newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kenya trying to contact Moslem preacher in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Kenya trying to contact Moslem preacher in Germany.

text.p: Kenya's embassy in Bonn said on Friday it had not managed to contact a Moslem preacher and critic of President Daniel arap Moi to tell him he was free to go home after two years of forced exile in Germany.
Ambassador Vincent Ogutu-Obare told Reuters his office had tried to contact Sheikh Khalid Balala since Thursday, when Kenya reversed its earlier stand not to allow the fiery preacher back home.

"We have tried to reach him without success," Ogutu-Obare said. "The embassy has been requested to assist him to go back home, to facilitate his return. He will be given the travel documents when he presents himself to us."
Attempts by Reuters on Friday to contact Balala in Frankfurt, where he has been living, were unsuccessful.

Analysts say the return of Balala, who commands a large following in Kenya's coastal region, will provide a major boost for the country's opposition in presidential and parliamentary elections this year.
Balala, speaking from Frankfurt last week, threatened to launch popular unprisings and industrial unrest in Kenya if Moi, seeking re-election this year, did not agree to step down.

Balala had also threatened to enter the country illegally and wage an armed struggle to bring down Moi's government, which he brands oppressive and likens to that of ousted Zairean dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.
Balala was refused entry to Kenya on June 7, when security officers detained him on arrival in the coastal resort of Mombasa and forced him to return to Germany.
He said his Kenyan passport had expired while he was in Germany but the Kenyan embassy refused to renew it. He said he had German travel documents but remained a Kenyan citizen.

Moi and Kenyan immigration officials have said Balala, who has a Kenyan mother and Yemeni father, automatically gave up his Kenyan citizenship when he failed to renounce his Yemeni citizenship at the age of 21.
Moi, aged 73 and in power since 1978, must call elections in 1997 pitting the ruling KANU party against an opposition fractured mainly along ethnic and personal lines.
The opposition has called for peaceful rallies across the country on Monday to press for constitutional reforms Moi has refused to carry out.
